name: Autoscaling
intent: Add and remove instances automatically from a metric, so capacity follows traffic without paying for the peak all day.
scenario: A web tier of 2 instances sits behind a load balancer. A promotion sends traffic from 100 to 1000 requests per second within minutes, then it fades into a quiet night. Each instance serves 100 requests per second and needs 2 minutes to warm up.
problem: Traffic is not flat. Fixed capacity sized for the peak wastes money for most of the day, and capacity sized for the average falls over during a spike. A person watching a graph and clicking a button reacts in tens of minutes, long after users have felt it. But automating it is not free: new instances take time to become useful, so a controller that reacts to a metric is always a little behind, and one that reacts too eagerly oscillates.

howItWorks.title: Measure a metric that tracks load
howItWorks.text: The autoscaler reads a metric from the monitoring system, usually averaged over a minute: CPU utilisation, requests per instance from the load balancer, or queue depth for workers. The best metric rises when the fleet needs more capacity, falls when it needs less, and scales with the number of instances. CPU is easy but saturates at 100%, so it cannot say how far over capacity you are.

howItWorks.title: Choose a policy
howItWorks.text: Target tracking keeps a metric near a value (for example 60% CPU or 600 requests per instance) and computes the instance count itself, like a thermostat. Step scaling adds or removes fixed amounts when thresholds are crossed (add 1 above 70%, add 4 above 90%). Scheduled scaling sets the count at known times, such as before a daily peak or a sale. Real systems often combine a schedule for the predictable part with target tracking for the rest.

howItWorks.title: Launch, warm up, then count
howItWorks.text: A scale-out asks the cloud for instances, which boot, start the app, load caches and pass health checks. That is typically 30 seconds for a pre-built container and several minutes for a full VM image. Until the load balancer sees them healthy they serve nothing, though they are billed. Good controllers account for instances that are warming so they do not launch again for the same gap.

howItWorks.title: Cooldown and scale-in caution
howItWorks.text: After an action, a cooldown (often 1 to 5 minutes, close to the warm-up time) stops the controller acting again before it can see the effect. Scale-in is made slower than scale-out on purpose: require the metric to stay low for a while, remove a few instances at a time, and let instances finish work. Scale-in protection can also exclude specific instances, such as one finishing a long job, from being terminated.

howItWorks.title: Bound the result
howItWorks.text: A minimum keeps a safe floor (at least 2, in different zones, so one failure is not an outage) and avoids cold-start on the first request after a quiet night. A maximum caps cost and protects downstream services, since 200 instances can overwhelm a database that was built for 20. Alert when the fleet sits at the maximum: the autoscaler has run out of room.

pros: Pays for roughly the capacity the traffic needs instead of the peak all day
Absorbs growth and spikes without a person in the loop
Replaces failed instances as a side effect of keeping the count
Pairs naturally with immutable images and an orchestrator
cons: Always reacts after the fact: warm-up time is a window of overload
Wrong metric, target or cooldown gives overload or flapping, and is hard to notice in quiet times
Needs stateless (or at least easily movable) instances and fast, repeatable start-up
Can pass the problem downstream: more web instances means more database connections and more load on dependencies
A cost surprise is possible: a bug, bot or attack can scale you to the maximum
whenToUse: Variable or unpredictable traffic with stateless instances behind a load balancer
Queue workers whose backlog grows and shrinks
Daily or weekly peaks that a schedule can cover, with target tracking on top for surprises
whenNotToUse: Flat, predictable load where a fixed fleet is simpler and often cheaper with reserved pricing
Stateful systems that are hard to resize, such as a primary database or a sharded store with expensive rebalancing
When start-up takes longer than the spikes last: keep headroom or use a queue to absorb them instead
When the bottleneck is downstream: adding web instances only makes the database fall over faster
pitfalls: Scaling on CPU for an I/O-bound service whose CPU stays low while latency climbs, or on a metric that saturates and hides the size of the spike
Cooldown shorter than the warm-up, so the controller keeps launching for a gap that is already being filled, then scales back in hard
Scaling in as fast as scaling out: noisy traffic around the target makes the fleet launch and kill instances all day and pay for warm-ups it never uses
Averaging the metric over cold instances, which dilutes it and delays the response (or reads their startup CPU spike as real load)
No maximum, or one so high a spike or bug becomes a huge bill and floods a database; a minimum of 1 means one failure is an outage
Terminating an instance mid-request or mid-job: use connection draining and scale-in protection
Testing only with gradual load: a real spike is the test that exposes warm-up lag

roles.label: Users
roles.description: Demand that rises and falls, sometimes sharply.

roles.label: Load balancer
roles.description: Spreads requests over the instances it sees as healthy, and reports requests per instance.

roles.label: Web tier
roles.description: The pool of identical stateless instances whose size changes.

roles.label: Metrics
roles.description: Collects and averages load measurements such as CPU or requests per instance.

roles.label: Autoscaler
roles.description: Compares the metric to the policy, applies cooldown and bounds, and asks the platform to add or remove instances.

quiz.question: A service scales out when average CPU is above 70%. Its instances take 4 minutes to boot and the cooldown is 30 seconds. During a spike, the fleet launches new instances every 30 seconds, then ends up far too large and scales back in. What is the best fix?
options: Lower the CPU target so that the controller starts launching instances earlier
Scale in as fast as it scales out, so that the cost drops back quickly after a spike
Set the cooldown near the warm-up time and count warming instances
Add a second metric, such as memory, that also triggers extra launches during a spike
quiz.explanation: The controller is acting before it can see the effect of its last action. Matching cooldown to warm-up stops the over-launch. Faster scale-in would worsen the oscillation, and a lower target or a second metric only launches sooner, not more wisely.

quiz.question: An I/O-bound API server spends most of its time waiting on a database. Under heavy load, latency climbs from 80 ms to 2 s while CPU stays at 25%. The autoscaler uses a CPU target of 60%. Which change is the best?
options: Lower the CPU target to 20% so that it triggers sooner when the latency starts to rise
Raise the maximum instance count so that the CPU figure has room to climb
Switch to scheduled scaling at hourly intervals based on the usual daily traffic shape
Scale on requests per instance, which keeps rising as load rises
quiz.explanation: CPU does not track load for this service, so the target never triggers. A 20% target would scale constantly in normal times and still miss real overload. A higher maximum does not move CPU, and an hourly schedule ignores the actual load.

quiz.question: A fleet autoscales a stateless web tier from 4 to 120 instances. During a flash sale it reaches 120 and the orders database, sized for about 30 web instances, falls over. What is the best lesson?
options: Set a maximum the database can cope with, and alert when the fleet reaches it
Remove the maximum so that the fleet can always keep up with demand during a sale
Increase the cooldown so that fewer instances are launched at the same time
Scale in faster so that instances are removed again before they overload the database
quiz.explanation: More web instances only push more load onto a fixed-size dependency. A maximum protects it, and alerting at the maximum shows when the fleet has run out of room.
